record.title: A Carnegie Mellon study maps when TypeSafe JEV can replace or defer expensive LLM judges
record.summary: Li, Miao, Krishnan and Padman evaluate hosted TypeSafe JEV 1.13.0 as a decision-only LLM judge and as the first stage of a confidence-based cascade. Across 5,172 judgments and selected public benchmarks, the authors report JEV near GPT-6 on several text-readable tasks at a fraction of its fee and a 0.15-second median latency, but materially behind on difficult correctness tasks such as math, code and logic. A threshold frozen before testing routes uncertain decisions to GPT-6: the paper reports 0.9 percentage points above GPT-6 on 1,610 held-out pairs at 41% of the fee, and exact GPT-6 accuracy on a pre-specified 570-pair live test across two new workloads while escalating 74% at 25% of the fee. The boundary matters: confidence error detection weakens on style-adversarial examples, and JEV and other tested judges are near chance yet confident on a small reference-free prose sample. These are author-reported results from one JEV version and selected workloads, not a general guarantee for production evaluation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ v4 study of TypeSafe JEV 1.13.0 across 5,172 judgments and a selected set of 16 other judges, JEV ranked eighth among fifteen LLM judges pooled over 4,850 public judgments, 1.7 percentage points behind GPT-6, while costing about 0.36% as much and returning a median response in 0.15 seconds.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: With a confidence threshold frozen before held-out evaluation, a two-order JEV-to-GPT-6 cascade reportedly scored 0.9 points above GPT-6 on 1,610 held-out pairs at 41% of its fee; a pre-specified live test on two new workloads (570 pairs) matched GPT-6 accuracy while escalating 74% and using 25% of its fee.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The study reports that confidence routing weakens on style-adversarial pairs (error-detection AUROC 0.76 versus 0.84 on style-matched pairs) and is unusable on a small reference-free prose sample where all tested judges are near chance yet confident.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper identifies its measured system as TypeSafe JEV 1.13.0, a hosted decision-only service returning typed label probabilities, and reports blinded human adjudication for benchmark-label disagreements in a 990-item subset.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent group reproduced the comparisons, cascade policy, fee accounting or human-adjudication analysis; the study evaluates one proprietary JEV version and labels/results are author-managed.

Transfer to current JEV versions, operational distributions, non-English tasks and high-stakes decision costs is unknown; the paper reports failure on style-adversarial and reference-free prose samples.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported selective-judging profile transfers to real evaluation workloads, it could preserve much of a strong LLM judge’s accuracy at lower cost and latency; the impact is meaningful for evaluation pipelines, but the evidence is one paper using one proprietary JEV version and bounded test distributions.
limitations: The paper evaluates one proprietary JEV version against selected judges that differ in size, reasoning effort and serving; this is not a compute-matched comparison, and training overlap with benchmarks is unknown.
Decision-only judging omits explanations and extended deliberation; specialized professional domains were not tested.
Thresholds target a fixed accuracy tolerance rather than explicit cost of wrong verdicts versus escalation; only serial escalation to an independent judge is tested.
The 1,610-pair held-out cascade and 570-pair prospective live test are bounded workload samples; neither establishes a deployment guarantee.
Confidence routing weakens on style-adversarial pairs and fails on reference-free prose, where every tested judge is near chance yet confident.
Blinded human adjudication is used for benchmark-label disagreements in a 990-item subset, but the wider evaluation still depends on selected benchmarks and source labels.
The offline reproducibility package was not run or independently audited in this activation.

brief.summary: Li, Miao, Krishnan and Padman evaluate hosted TypeSafe JEV 1.13.0 as a decision-only LLM judge and as the first stage of a confidence-based cascade. Across 5,172 judgments and selected public benchmarks, the authors report JEV near GPT-6 on several text-readable tasks at a fraction of its fee and a 0.15-second median latency, but materially behind on difficult correctness tasks such as math, code and logic. A threshold frozen before testing routes uncertain decisions to GPT-6: the paper reports 0.9 percentage points above GPT-6 on 1,610 held-out pairs at 41% of the fee, and exact GPT-6 accuracy on a pre-specified 570-pair live test across two new workloads while escalating 74% at 25% of the fee. The boundary matters: confidence error detection weakens on style-adversarial examples, and JEV and other tested judges are near chance yet confident on a small reference-free prose sample. These are author-reported results from one JEV version and selected workloads, not a general guarantee for production evaluation.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that JEV 1.13.0 is close to GPT-6 on several text-readable evaluation tasks for a small fraction of its fee, and that a frozen confidence cascade can match or slightly exceed GPT-6 on selected held-out/live workloads while lowering fees. These are paper-reported comparative results.
technical.compute_or_cost: For the measured JEV version, the paper reports $0.044 per 1,000 judgments and 0.15-second median latency. The frozen held-out cascade reportedly costs 41% of GPT-6; the prospective two-workload cascade costs 25%. Fees are estimates from reported usage and collection-time pricing, not invoices.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v4 paper publicly describes a 5,172-judgment study, 16 comparison judges, blinded human adjudication on a 990-item disagreement subset, held-out routing and two pre-specified new workloads. This activation inspected the manuscript but did not rerun the analysis or service calls.
technical.implementation_status: The study evaluates hosted JEV 1.13.0; external replication and current-version transfer were not assessed.
technical.mechanism: JEV returns a decision distribution over typed labels; the highest label probability is used as confidence. A threshold selected on labeled workload-specific data accepts high-confidence JEV verdicts and sends the remainder to an independent GPT-6 judge.
technical.regime: JEV 1.13.0 on pairwise preference, evidence-grounded factuality and final-answer judgments, with follow-ups for style, harder correctness, format and natural prose. Main cascade results use public benchmark subsets and two new correctness workloads; they do not establish performance across professional domains or high-stakes deployment.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links an offline package that reproduces principal analyses from retained outputs and supplies prospective protocols, requests, thresholds, runners and records. This activation did not execute the package or independently audit data and label provenance.
technical.strongest_baseline: GPT-6 is the paper’s main reasoning-judge baseline under the same decision/probability output contract. Sixteen hosted and reward-model judges are compared, but the systems differ in size, reasoning effort, serving and computation; the authors explicitly do not claim a compute-matched comparison.

brief.title: A Carnegie Mellon study maps when TypeSafe JEV can replace or defer expensive LLM judges
brief.why_it_matters: This provides an external, task-bounded test of whether a low-cost typed decision model can reserve expensive reasoning for uncertain evaluations. If reproduced on local workloads, confidence-based escalation could lower the recurring cost and latency of large-scale model evaluation. The paper also shows where the approach breaks: difficult derived judgments, adversarial answer style and reference-free factuality need stronger checking or abstention.

other.title: TypeSafe introduces Jev, a structured decision model with first-party workflow evaluations
other.summary: TypeSafe introduced Jev, an early-access model it describes as a fast structured-decision system using typed probability outputs, parallel sampling and RLCD training. Its company-run evaluation site compares Jev and other models on four authored workflows; TypeSafe reports favorable accuracy/cost and accuracy/time frontiers and advertises peak comparisons of 193.6x lower cost and 444.6x faster, while saying those gains are near the high end of expected real-world results. The comparison uses GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 high-reasoning outputs averaged as reference labels, with other models at provider-default reasoning, and assumes the workflow harness is correct. TypeSafe says the task content was authored by its model-capabilities team and that wrapper constraints affect other models' costs and speed. The reported advantage is therefore a first-party result on four workflows, not an independent or ground-truth validation of broad automation performance. Its 0% type-error figure is guaranteed by schema matching and is not an empirical accuracy result.
